groups.sub: Seven things he deletes that a lesser writer keeps. This is where the succinctness you admire actually comes from - not from short words, from removed material.

m.d: Quoted dialogue is reserved for emotional turns and decisions. Anything logistical - a refusal, an agreement, a plan - gets one line of reported speech. A whole refusal scene lands in fourteen words. A lesser writer stages both.
m.t: Take a scene with full dialogue. Any exchange conveying procedure becomes one reported sentence. Only exchanges where somebody changes their mind keep quotation marks.

m.n: State the outcome, delete the deliberation
m.d: He never writes the internal weighing of an option the reader can already predict. The reader has just watched the argument that produces the decision, so the decision itself takes four words.
m.t: Find every paragraph where a character or you decides something. Cut the weighing. Keep the verdict.

m.d: Standard rhythm is line, reaction, line. He runs line, line. In one 2024 book, 100 adjacent dialogue turns carry no tag and no beat at all. A beat appears only when it does work a line cannot.
m.t: Write a 20-turn argument. Only 'said', at most five times. At most three physical beats, each carrying information no line of dialogue does.

m.d: A person is established by a single fact, then the scene proceeds. No portrait, no head-to-toe description on entry. Description arrives only in the clause where it matters.
m.t: Introduce five people in one sentence each. One fact only. The fact must pre-explain their behaviour for the next paragraph.

m.n: Emotion named once, flatly, then dropped
m.d: A heart is 'a bit heavy'. Someone is 'in complete shock'. No elaboration, no physicalisation, no simile. He never writes a paragraph about how somebody feels. The understatement is the effect.
m.t: Take your most emotional paragraph. Reduce the emotion to one flat clause. Delete everything that elaborates it.

m.d: He quantifies where a weaker writer amplifies: 2,500 miles, 48 minutes, 10,000 fruits, 53 mantras. 'Very' appears about 41 times in 48,000 words. The number carries the awe; the adjective would only assert it.
m.t: Replace every intensifier in a draft with a specific number. Odd numbers, not round ones - round reads as estimate, odd reads as record.

m.d: Where a teaching would need a paragraph of theory, he writes one compressed line instead. The aphorism IS the compression of the argument, not a decoration on top of it.
m.t: Find a paragraph of yours that explains a principle. Replace the whole paragraph with one sentence under fifteen words. Keep it only if nothing is lost.

groups.sub: Six ways he raises a question and refuses to answer it. This is where the profundity comes from: the prose reads as knowing more than it says.

m.d: Closes a motive question without answering it. A character was 'just being' himself. The question is acknowledged and shut in one clause.
m.t: Raise a why. Answer it with a restatement of the subject. Move on without apologising.

m.d: He will hold an open question across a chapter boundary rather than pay it off cheaply. A question raised at the end of chapter three is answered a full chapter later.
m.t: Ask a real question at the end of a section. Answer it two sections later, not in the next paragraph.

m.d: He truncates a famous story mid-summary and points you at the source rather than retelling it. The refusal to retell signals that he could.
m.t: Name a story your reader half-knows. Give three sentences. Point them at the full version and stop.

m.d: Four scriptural versions of a birth are named in one sentence. He picks none. An alternative etymology is given, then dropped.
m.t: Find a contested point. State the two or three live positions in one sentence each. Pick none. Continue.

m.d: He asserts that further reasons exist and withholds them. The existence of more is stated; the more is not supplied.
m.t: Assert that there are other reasons for something. Name one. Leave the rest stated but unlisted.

m.d: Rather than describing something as beyond description, he states plainly that it was an enigma to fathom, and does not then attempt to fathom it. Note the difference from 'words cannot describe', which he never writes.
m.t: Take something you were about to over-describe. Say once that it could not be worked out. Then say nothing more about it.

groups.sub: Five substitutes for adjective-stacking. Measured across the mythic set-pieces where a lesser writer would reach for radiant, resplendent, magnificent.

m.d: A billion galaxies. A thousand constellations. A firefly in front of a billion suns. The figure does the work an adjective would only claim.
m.t: Ten moments of overwhelming scale. Every one built on a count, never on an adjective.

m.d: He does not say the venom was terrible. He says one spilled drop turned several thousand miles of land barren, the plants wilted, the fruit went black. You infer the magnitude from the damage.
m.t: Describe something powerful only by what it did to things around it. The thing itself gets no adjectives.

m.d: His reliable move at every sacred moment is that motion stops. Time stands still, silence descends, the universe holds its breath. Awe is written as an absence of sound and movement, not a pile of light-words.
m.t: Write ten peaks. Each is built from a cessation of motion or sound, one specific material detail, and one number. Ban every glow word.

m.d: Not an ornament but earrings made from purified mercury. Not a bowl but an inverted skull cut into the shape of one. Not trees but teak, deodar, sandalwood. The named material carries what the adjective would fake.
m.t: Go through a description and replace every category noun with a named material or species.

m.d: His default noun phrase. Where three adjectives appear they are almost always inside dialogue or in the two deliberately excessive passages that are his weakest writing. Do not model on those.
m.t: Cap yourself at one adjective per noun phrase for a whole draft. Add a fact where the second adjective was.

groups.sub: How he makes a hard idea feel easy. The three-beat unit runs 40 to 80 times per chapter and is the single most copyable thing in the teaching books.

m.d: State the point flat and abstract in under fifteen words. Show one concrete physical object. Then state the point AGAIN using the object's own noun. Almost everyone does claim-then-image and stops. The third beat is what turns an image into an explanation.
m.t: Fifteen abstract claims, three sentences each. Cover the first sentence: the third must still deliver the whole claim.

m.d: He names the wrong mental model first, as a physical object, then the right one. This makes the analogy do argumentative work instead of decoration. It also tells the reader what to stop believing, which is more useful than what to start believing.
m.t: For each claim, name the wrong object your reader is already running, then the right one, then one sentence on what the right one does that the wrong one cannot.

m.d: Kitchens, tamed animals, small children, weather, machines you have physically operated. Never aviation, physics, war, neuroscience, software. Explaining a high idea with a washing machine is a status transaction: it says the idea is not above you.
m.t: List twelve analogies. Ban any vehicle more impressive than its subject. If the source costs more than a few hundred rupees, pick again.

m.d: Median analogy length is one to two sentences. He has no extended conceits and never calls an image back three pages later. Cuteness is a function of over-extension.
m.t: Find every metaphor in a draft. Cut everything past sentence two. Delete every callback.

m.n: The analogy carries a rule, not a mood
m.d: Brewing coffee does not mean anger is unpleasant. It means anger gets bitter past a specific point and cannot be sweetened afterwards. The image supplies a rule that survives the image being forgotten.
m.t: Delete the image from each of your analogies. If nothing survives, you wrote decoration.

groups.sub: Seven joke machines. The placement rule matters more than the joke: last in the paragraph, shortest in the paragraph, unsignalled.

m.d: A flat two or three word qualifier dropped immediately after a hyperbole he has just committed. Self-audit as comedy.
m.t: Commit a small exaggeration. Undercut it in the next three words.

m.n: Register clash, resolved in one sentence
m.d: An ancient or sacred frame, punctured by a mundane commercial object: a pay grade, a chequebook, a private jet, a twenty-rupee torch. The joke is the collision, and it always lands in final position.
m.t: Twelve paragraphs on a serious subject. Each ends on the shortest sentence, importing one cheap modern object.

m.d: Setup, turn, tag - each strictly shorter than the last. Seven words, then two, then four. The arithmetic IS the timing.
m.t: Twenty three-sentence jokes with strictly descending lengths. Count them. Remove the third sentence and the joke should get worse.

m.d: A mouse becomes Master Mouse. One capital letter, no explanation, no follow-up. The joke is that he does not acknowledge the joke.
m.t: Give something small a title it has not earned. Never mention it again.

m.d: The punchline is a character taking a figure of speech at face value - and it is the same error the reader is making. That is why the joke teaches instead of merely relieving.
m.t: Ten two-hander jokes where the punchline is a literal reading, spoken by the lower-status character.

m.d: One word, aimed upward, after a run of misfortune. Never aimed at the reader.
m.t: After three things go wrong, react in one word. Do not explain it.

m.d: The butt is almost always the teacher, the master, the expert, or himself. He comes last at go-karting; he puts a retraction in a headline. Having paid that, he can write an absolute sentence and it reads as observation, not sermon.
m.t: If a joke's target is your reader or your customer, cut it. If your piece has no joke at your own expense, you have not paid for your strongest claim.

groups.sub: Five understatement mechanisms, measured against events that would justify enormous language.

m.d: End an ecstatic passage on a clock reading or a date, not a reflection. The most transcendent event in a 52,000-word book closes on the time on his watch. The number re-anchors the reader at the exact moment the prose could inflate.
m.t: Write 250 words on your most intense experience. The last sentence is a clock time or a measurement, nothing else.

m.d: A flat two to five word summary supplied immediately after the peak. Months of extreme austerity get summarised in two words.
m.t: After each peak, one flat verdict of five words or fewer. It may not describe.

m.d: He states outright that he is understating, and then does not compensate for it later. Saying so is not permission to inflate afterwards.
m.t: Say once that you are underselling something. Then never upgrade the language.

m.d: Cosmic events compared to household failure: a swollen wooden door, starched cloth that will not soak, salt thrown on ice cream.
m.t: Compare your largest experience to something that goes wrong in a kitchen.

m.n: Refuse the superlative, assert reality instead
m.d: Where a superlative is due he substitutes an absence: there was no doubt it was as real as the floor he sat on. Reality, not glory, is the claim.
m.t: Replace every superlative with a statement about how real the thing was.

m.d: Every high is followed inside one paragraph by something that costs him - a failure, a chore, a doubt, something the peak broke. Never two crescendos in a row.
m.t: Five peaks of 150 words. Each followed by a paragraph that costs you something concrete.

groups.sub: Six distinct patterns for six different jobs. Parentheses are almost never used - roughly six instances in a whole book against about eighty comma-appositives.

m.d: The default and by far the most frequent. Term, then a one to six word noun phrase, commas both sides, sentence continues. The gloss is grammatically disposable: delete it and the sentence still parses. That is exactly why it does not feel like teaching.
m.t: Twenty-five terms from your own field. Gloss each inline in six words or fewer. Delete every gloss afterwards - all twenty-five must still be grammatical.

m.d: The unfamiliar word becomes the predicate, and what follows is not a synonym but a rendered picture. Teaches the feel of a word rather than its dictionary value, and it stacks - three or four in a row build a portrait entirely out of glossed terms.
m.t: Describe someone using only unfamiliar terms, each immediately cashed as an image rather than a definition.

m.d: Used when the concept matters more than the label. The plain phrase leads, the term follows as a name for what you already understand.
m.t: Introduce five concepts plain-first. The term arrives only after the reader already holds the idea.

m.d: He glosses by telling you how the word was earned, which converts vocabulary into plot. A name is conferred by an event rather than defined.
m.t: Ten terms. For each, a 40-80 word scene in which the name is earned, ending on the naming sentence.

m.d: Devotional exclamations, mantra fragments and epithet-floods are never glossed. The reader is trusted to absorb them as sound, because the point is texture, not semantics.
m.t: Leave one term unglossed on purpose, where the sound matters more than the meaning.

m.d: He does not assume retention. The same term is re-glossed on later appearances in the same disposable form. Cost: two words. Benefit: no chapter requires having read the previous one.
m.t: Re-gloss your key term the second and third time it appears. Do not assume the reader remembers.
